questions.stem:
If Rousseau were to critically evaluate Locke's account of the social contract and natural rights, he would most
        likely argue that:

options.label: a
options.text:
Locke's social contract is essentially sound because both thinkers ground political legitimacy in the consent
            of individuals, making their accounts of legitimate authority more complementary than contradictory.

options.label: b
options.text:
The protection of individual natural rights particularly the right to property constitutes a sufficient and
            complete basis for legitimate government, rendering any further appeal to a collective general will
            philosophically unnecessary.

options.label: c
options.text:
Locke's supreme legislature successfully approximates the expression of the general will, since it derives its
            authority from collective consent and remains accountable to the people through the right of dissolution.

options.label: d
options.text:
Grounding political legitimacy in the protection of individual natural rights and especially the right to
            property serves primarily the interests of those who already possess property, and cannot generate the
            genuine common good that the general will requires.

questions.stem:
According to the description of Rousseau's argument, which of the following most accurately captures the
        distinction between the "general will" and the "will of all"?

options.label: a
options.text:
The general will be expressed through formally elected representative institutions, whereas the will of all
            refers to the unmediated and direct preferences of citizens expressed in open democratic assemblies.

options.label: b
options.text:
The general will encompasses the totality of individual preferences when aggregated through majority voting
            procedures, whereas the will of all refers to the moral preferences of a virtuous minority possessing superior
            civic judgment.

options.label: c
options.text:
The general will represents the collective rational interest of the community as a whole, whereas the will of
            all is merely the aggregation of private individual interests that may or may not align with the common good.

Passage (Q.10-Q.18): The resilience of liberal democracy rests on a delicate equipoise between two competing
        impulses: the principle of majority rule and the constraints imposed by constitutionalism. Majority rule,
        grounded in the egalitarian notion that each citizen’s preference carries equal weight, is the engine of democratic
        legitimacy. Yet, without counter-majoritarian safeguards—an independent judiciary, entrenched rights, and a
        free press—the very mechanism that empowers the majority can devour the preconditions for meaningful
        participation. This is the paradox of democracy: its procedural core, if left unchecked, can erode its own liberal
        substance.
        In recent decades, a resurgent populism has weaponized this internal tension. While populist leaders claim to
        speak for the people, their assault on independent institutions ultimately silences the very voices they purport to
        amplify. Populist leaders, cloaking themselves in the language of the ‘will of the people,’ portray constitutional
        checks as elitist obstacles to authentic popular sovereignty. By equating electoral victory with an unbounded
        mandate, they delegitimize institutions that temper transient majorities. The rhetoric is seductive: why should
        unelected judges or a critical press override the voice of the demos? Yet, this framing masks a deeper illiberalism.
        Stripped of liberal guardrails, majoritarianism can transmute into plebiscitary autocracy, where rights become
        contingent on the whim of the current majority, and dissent is branded as treachery.
        Economists and political theorists have long noted that the erosion of democratic norms is often gradual, not
        cataclysmic. It begins not with the tanks but with the subtle hollowing of institutional credibility. When the press
        is derided as an enemy of the people, when judicial independence is framed as an affront to popular will, the
        epistemic foundations of democracy crack. Citizens lose the shared factual basis for deliberation, and the public
        sphere fractures into echo chambers of partisan truth. The result is a governance by acclamation, where the
        substance of democracy is supplanted by its pageantry.
        Paradoxically, restoring equilibrium requires a revitalization of the very constitutional ethos that populism
        scorns. This is not a call for judicial oligarchy but for a deeper civic understanding that democracy is more than
        an electoral arithmetic. It is a normative commitment to the dignity of all, a recognition that the majority’s
        legitimacy is bounded by the rights of those it temporarily outnumbers. Until this conception is widely
        re-embraced, liberal democracy will remain, in the words of one philosopher, “a promise constantly betrayed by
        its own success.”

Passage (Q.19-Q.26): The proliferation of algorithmic risk assessment tools in criminal justice has been
        heralded as a triumph of data-driven objectivity. Yet beneath the veneer of mathematical precision lies a tangled
        web of normative judgments, opaque design, and institutional inertia. These instruments, often marketed as
        neutral aids to judicial decision-making, encode assumptions about risk that are far from value-free. The
        variables selected—employment history, residential stability, prior encounters with law enforcement—are
        proxies that mirror structural inequalities, transforming socioeconomic disadvantage into a quantified predictor
        of future criminality. This is the quiet alchemy of actuarial justice: the transmutation of systemic failure into
        individual culpability.
        Critics argue that such tools do not merely reflect bias but actively launder it through the rhetoric of science.
        When a risk score is presented as a numerical output, it acquires an aura of objectivity that insulates it from the
        adversarial scrutiny fundamental to due process. The black-box nature of proprietary algorithms further
        compounds the problem, creating an epistemic asymmetry where the defendant is unable to challenge the logic
        that generated the score. This asymmetry is not a glitch but a feature of a system that prioritizes predictive
        efficiency over procedural fairness. Yet proponents counter that human judges are themselves riddled with
        cognitive biases, and that a consistent, albeit imperfect, algorithm may still outperform the vagaries of intuition.
        The appeal is seductive: replace the fallible human with the dispassionate machine.
        The deeper danger, however, is not that algorithms might make occasional errors, but that their integration
        reshapes the very telos of the justice system. When the goal shifts from adjudicating guilt and moral desert to
        managing aggregate risk, the courtroom ceases to be a site of individualized justice and becomes a sorting
        mechanism for dangerous populations. The presumption of innocence, already fragile, is further eroded when a
        defendant is prefaced by a score. Regulation lags, as lawmakers grapple with the tension between proprietary
        innovation and public accountability. Meaningful oversight requires not just audits of disparate impact, but a
        fundamental interrogation of whether some decisions are simply inappropriate for algorithmic delegation. The
        choice is not between human and machine, but between justice as a moral enterprise and justice as a bureaucratic
        optimization problem.
        —Adapted from “Algorithmic Injustice: Risk Assessment and the Erosion of Due Process,” Harvard Law Review
        Forum, 2023.
